title: Venezuela's Acting President Is in India to Sell Oil. The Hormuz Crisis Made This Visit Inevitable.
excerpt: Delcy Rodríguez's five-day visit comes as India becomes the second-largest buyer of Venezuelan crude, importing 427,000 barrels per day to offset the Strait of Hormuz shutdown.
body:
Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodríguez arrived in India on Tuesday for a five-day working visit that is less about diplomacy and more about survival arithmetic. India needs oil. Venezuela has oil. The Strait of Hormuz — through which more than 40 percent of India's crude imports once flowed — is effectively closed. The math writes itself.

Rodríguez will meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi and hold talks spanning energy, trade, investment, pharmaceuticals, healthcare, transportation, and renewable energy, according to India's Ministry of External Affairs. She is also expected to meet leaders of India's energy industry in Mumbai, including executives from Reliance Industries, which has emerged as one of the world's three largest buyers of Venezuelan crude.

## Why Venezuela, Why Now

India was the second-largest importer of Venezuelan oil in May, purchasing 427,000 barrels per day — second only to the United States. That figure would have been unthinkable a year ago. India had stopped buying Venezuelan crude entirely after Trump authorised a 25 percent discretionary tariff on countries purchasing from Caracas. It resumed purchases in February 2026, after sanctions were eased following a landmark oil supply pact between Washington and Caracas.

The arrangement that makes this possible is unusual. Under the agreement reached after the U.S. capture of former President Nicolás Maduro in January, Washington controls the proceeds from Venezuelan oil sales through Treasury-administered bank accounts. Commercial terms also follow U.S. guidance. Venezuela sells the oil; America controls the money.

For India, this arrangement offers a politically clean alternative to Middle Eastern crude. Venezuelan oil does not transit the Strait of Hormuz. It does not require Iranian permission to ship. And because the United States effectively supervises the transactions, there is no sanctions risk — a consideration that has weighed heavily on Indian refiners since the conflict began.

## The Hormuz Gap

The scale of India's energy problem is difficult to overstate. Before the U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, the Strait of Hormuz carried roughly 20 percent of the world's crude oil and refined products. For India specifically, the strait was the passage for more than 40 percent of its crude imports.

Three months later, that flow has slowed to a trickle. Asia's seaborne crude arrivals in May were 19.47 million barrels per day — down 22 percent from the pre-conflict average of 24.82 million bpd. The OECD warned on Wednesday that a prolonged disruption could push some Asian economies into recession.

India has responded by diversifying aggressively. Imports from the United States have more than doubled, reaching a record 2.05 million bpd in May, with 3.07 million bpd expected by July. Venezuelan crude fills another piece of the puzzle. State-run Hindustan Petroleum Corporation is reportedly exploring Venezuelan crude for the first time, signalling a shift in sourcing patterns that could become permanent.

## Rodríguez's Larger Agenda

The Venezuelan delegation includes ministers for foreign affairs, economy and finance, science and technology, communications, and transportation. That lineup suggests the visit is about more than oil. Venezuela has recently opened its electricity sector to private investment through legislation that would allow joint ventures with the state holding a minimum 50 percent stake. Energy-intensive Indian companies could find opportunities in a country desperate for capital and infrastructure.

Rodríguez assumed the acting presidency after Venezuela's Supreme Court ordered her to take over following Maduro's detention. She last visited India in February 2025 as oil minister, leading a delegation to India Energy Week. Her return as head of state — even in an acting capacity — marks a significant elevation in the bilateral relationship.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs in the energy sector, the India-Venezuela corridor represents both opportunity and complexity. Reliance's Venezuelan operations are expanding. HPCL is entering new territory. The pipeline of Indian engineers and managers serving in Latin American energy markets is likely to grow.

The visit also underscores a broader reality: India's energy security now depends on relationships with countries most Indians have barely thought about. The era when the Gulf provided cheap, reliable crude is, for now, over. What replaces it will be messier, more expensive, and far more geographically scattered.
